case_studies.title: KaliBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Cybersecurity Tool Use on Kali Linux with Runtime-Free Verifiable Rewards
case_studies.abstract: LLMs are increasingly applied to cybersecurity workflows, where they are expected to translate analysts' intent into tool invocations. However, existing evaluations focus on knowledge-based assessments or end-to-end agentic tasks, and do not directly measure LLMs' ability to generate executable commands for real-world cybersecurity tools. This gap is critical because cybersecurity operations rely on strict command-line interfaces (CLIs), where minor syntax errors, incorrect flag--value bindings, or argument misordering can invalidate execution. We introduce KaliBench, a fine-grained benchmark
case_studies.summary: KaliBench measures how accurately large language models can produce correct command‑line instructions for real Kali Linux security tools, filling a gap where previous tests only checked general knowledge. It provides a detailed benchmark with 13,000 real‑world prompts and metrics that reveal current LLMs struggle with exact syntax. The result is a new standard for testing tool‑specific command generation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The benchmark is novel in its focus on fine-grained CLI command generation for Kali Linux, which is a common tool in security operations. IT engineers and consultants dealing with security tooling would find the ability to evaluate LLMs on realistic command syntax valuable. The benchmark provides actionable data that could be used to improve automation scripts, detect syntax vulnerabilities, and build better security tooling pipelines, making it useful within 90 days. Overall the paper scores well across all criteria.

case_studies.title: Groundability, Not Scale Alone: When Weak Reviewers Can Audit Strong Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: Coding agents can return plausible patches that omit required behavior. These failures are hard to review because long traces and confident summaries often hide what was missed. We ask when a nominally weaker reviewer can reliably decide whether a patch solves its issue. We study 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents and 101 controlled cases. On 154 GPT-5.4 traces, structured but unchecked evidence raises both defect catch and over-rejection. We then provide official execution evidence as an upper-bound diagnostic. After choosing and freezing one of two formats per reviewer, five of s
case_studies.summary: This research shows that even when code‑patching AI tools give convincing summaries, weaker reviewers can still catch errors by focusing on execution traces and a single agreed evidence format. They analysed 411 real and 101 controlled agent patches, finding that structured evidence improves defect detection but still risks over‑rejection. For cloud infra managers, this means you can reduce audit overhead by using the proposed evidence format to quickly spot missing behaviour in automated code fixes.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage automated patching or CI pipelines, here is what to do: 1) require developers or bots to attach a single, clear execution trace to each patch; 2) train reviewers to focus on that trace rather than summary logs; 3) stop approving patches that lack this trace – it reduces missed bugs and keeps review time low.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents practical insights into auditing AI-generated code patches, a topic directly relevant to software engineering teams managing large codebases and automated CI pipelines. The discussion of reviewer reliability, structured evidence, and execution traces offers actionable guidelines that IT engineers can adopt to improve code review workflows, especially when integrating LLM-based patch generators into their DevOps pipelines. While the academic depth is moderate, the practical implications are clear and can be leveraged within the next 90 days to reduce defect leakage and streamline review processes.

case_studies.title: cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents
case_studies.abstract: Computer use agents (CUAs), which use graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to complete tasks on a computer, have recently surpassed human performance on many standard benchmarks, including difficult long-horizon tasks. Their capabilities are undoubtedly impressive, however, a key barrier to the widespread adoption and deployment of CUAs remains their speed and cost. Progress towards faster yet capable CUAs requires reliable evaluation of their speed, but many CUA benchmarks currently face a reproducibility crisis. Benchmarks are based on complex infrastructure with varying machine and container co
case_studies.summary: The paper tackles the lack of reliable speed measurements for computer‑use agents (CUAs) by creating a standardized benchmark suite that runs on consistent hardware and software setups. They built a reproducible testing framework that measures how fast CUAs can perform GUI tasks, revealing that speed is still a major barrier to deployment. The result is a set of reproducible metrics that can help researchers identify hardware and software bottlenecks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a standardized benchmarking framework for evaluating the speed of computer‑use agents (GUI automation). This is a novel contribution that would interest IT engineers who rely on automation tools for tasks such as deployment, configuration, and monitoring. The framework could help them assess and compare the performance of existing automation solutions (e.g., Selenium, Playwright, or proprietary scripting engines) and guide procurement or development decisions. The direct relevance to daily IT operations is moderate; the benchmark itself is a research tool rather than a ready‑to‑deploy product, so the immediate actionable value within 90 days is limited. It could, however, inform future tooling or trigger internal pilots, justifying a short‑term use case.
